question: "Isn't the Bible full of contradictions, so it can't be trusted?"

sayings.quote: "...the scripture cannot be broken."
sayings.expo: Spoken while His opponents reached for stones. Defending Himself from one clause of one Psalm (82:6), He rested His whole case on the premise both sides accepted: Scripture cannot be broken -- luthēnai, loosed, untied, annulled. Not "is mostly reliable"; cannot fail. If the Scriptures were a self-contradicting patchwork, this argument collapses -- and He staked His life's defense on it holding.

sayings.quote: "Ye do err, not knowing the scriptures, nor the power of God."
sayings.expo: The Sadducees brought Him their era's version of a "gotcha contradiction" -- the woman widowed seven times. He did not concede a tangle in the text; He located the error in the reader: ye err. The diagnosis for an apparent contradiction is, first, insufficient knowledge of what the text actually says -- which is precisely the pattern with the internet's lists.

sayings.quote: "Have ye not read...?"
sayings.expo: His standing rebuttal -- He says it again and again (Matt 12:3, 12:5, 21:16, 21:42, 22:31). Every time a dispute arose, His remedy was go back and read the passage, and every time He treated what was written as decisive. He never once said "that part is corrupted" or "those accounts disagree." His practice is the verdict: the text, read, settles it.

reason: Most alleged contradictions dissolve exactly the way Christ modeled -- by reading the whole passage in its setting. The four Gospels are four witnesses of one life: witnesses who agree word-for-word are suspected of collusion; honest witnesses differ in detail and agree in substance, which is the mark of truth, not myth. So name the "contradiction," open the text, weigh the words in context -- few survive it.

question: "If God is loving and all-powerful, why does He allow suffering and evil?"

sayings.quote: "Neither hath this man sinned, nor his parents: but that the works of God should be made manifest in him."
sayings.expo: His own disciples assumed the skeptic's premise -- suffering must be somebody's punishment: "who sinned, this man or his parents?" Christ rejected the whole equation: neither. This blindness is not a verdict on anyone; it is an occasion for God's work to be shown. Suffering, in His teaching, is not proof of guilt -- and therefore not proof of an unloving God.

sayings.quote: "...those eighteen, upon whom the tower in Siloam fell... think ye that they were sinners above all men...? I tell you, Nay: but, except ye repent, ye shall all likewise perish."
sayings.expo: A real disaster -- a collapsed tower, eighteen dead -- put to Him directly. He refuses the karma-arithmetic twice ("I tell you, Nay"): the victims were not worse than anyone else. Then He turns the telescope around: the question tragedy should raise is not "what did they do?" but "where do I stand?" He treats catastrophe as a summons, never as a sum.

sayings.quote: "In the world ye shall have tribulation: but be of good cheer; I have overcome the world."
sayings.expo: Spoken the night before His own torture. He never promised a world without suffering -- He promised suffering, plainly, and then staked His claim on overcoming it, hours before absorbing the worst of it Himself. A faith whose founder predicts tribulation cannot be refuted by the existence of tribulation; and a God who walks into the suffering is the opposite of one aloof from it.

reason: God gave the will to choose -- love that cannot be refused is not love -- and most evil is that freedom misused. He does not author evil (James 1:13); He permits it for a season, works it toward good (Rom 8:28), and in the cross He does not watch pain from a distance but enters and bears it. The demand that He abolish all evil now, pressed honestly to its end, is the demand that choice and love be abolished with it.

question: "Would a loving God really send people to hell to be tortured forever?"

sayings.quote: "...fear him which is able to destroy both soul and body in hell."
sayings.expo: His single most direct statement of what hell does -- and the verb is destroy: apolesai, to bring to ruin, to end. Not "keep alive in torment forever." He even distinguishes it from what men can do ("kill the body") -- God's judgment reaches the whole person, and its outcome is destruction, not preservation in pain. The doctrine the skeptic finds monstrous is contradicted by the very verse that defines the stakes.

sayings.quote: "For God so loved the world... that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life."
sayings.expo: The most-quoted verse on earth is an either/or: perish or everlasting life. The contrast only works if the lost do not also live forever. If everyone lives eternally -- some in bliss, some in flame -- then everlasting life is not the gift that distinguishes the saved, and "perish" (apolētai, same root: be destroyed) means nothing. The verse's own logic requires that immortality is the gift, not the default.

sayings.quote: "...he will burn up the chaff with unquenchable fire."
sayings.expo: The picture chosen is chaff -- straw in fire. What does fire do to chaff? It burns it up; it does not roast it forever. "Unquenchable" describes the fire no one can put out until its work is done -- not fuel that never runs out. Every image in the teaching (chaff, weeds burned, a destroyed house, a perished soul) is an image of an end, not an endless middle.

reason: The wage of sin is death (Rom 6:23), immortality is a gift sought (Rom 2:7), and the Father is longsuffering, willing that none perish (2 Pet 3:9). "Everlasting punishment" is everlasting in its result -- a destruction never reversed -- as "eternal judgment" is a judgment never overturned. The "moral monster" is a man-made creed, not Christ's teaching; answer it with His own words and it falls.

question: "Is the Trinity biblical?"

sayings.quote: "And this is life eternal, that they might know thee the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom thou hast sent."
sayings.expo: This is prayer -- Christ speaking to the Father, no audience to simplify for. He calls the Father "the only true God" (monon alēthinon theon) and then names Himself separately, as the one sent. If the Son were co-equally the "only true God," the sentence would exclude Himself from deity in the act of defining eternal life. The prayer only reads naturally one way: the Father alone is the Most High, and knowing both Him and His sent One is life.

sayings.quote: "...my Father is greater than I."
sayings.expo: Four words that co-equality cannot digest: greater than I. Not "greater in office while equal in essence" -- that distinction appears nowhere in the text; it was built centuries later to protect the formula from the verse. He says it as comfort: the disciples should rejoice He goes to the Father, because the Father is greater. The statement is only comforting if it is simply true.

sayings.quote: "I ascend unto my Father, and your Father; and to my God, and your God."
sayings.expo: After the resurrection -- glorified, victorious -- He still calls the Father "my God." Whoever has a God is not the Most High Himself. And He deliberately parallels it with ours: my Father and your Father, my God and your God -- the same relation, His by nature and firstness, ours by adoption. The risen Christ worships; the Father is worshiped.

reason: The word "Trinity" never appears in Scripture; three co-equal persons was defined at Nicaea in 325 AD, centuries after the apostles. Scripture's own summary is one God, the Father, and one Lord, Yeshua the sent Son (1 Cor 8:6); the Holy Spirit is God's own breath and power, not a third person. To read co-equals into the text is to add to it what Christ's own prayer never said.

question: "Is Jesus God, co-equal with the Father?"

sayings.quote: "I can of mine own self do nothing..."
sayings.expo: He surrenders initiative: nothing from Himself; He judges as He hears, seeks not His own will but the will of Him that sent Him. An omnipotent co-equal cannot say "I can do nothing of myself" and mean it. This is the language of a Son whose power is real but derived -- given, sent, entrusted.

sayings.quote: "But of that day and that hour knoweth no man... neither the Son, but the Father."
sayings.expo: He surrenders knowledge: there is a fact the Father knows that the Son, then, did not. Co-equality's usual escape -- "He knew it as God but not as man" -- makes Christ's plain statement a technicality, and puts a distinction in His mouth He never made. He simply ranked the knowing: the Father above all.

sayings.quote: "...all men should honour the Son, even as they honour the Father... which hath sent him."
sayings.expo: And yet -- full honor to the Son. Notice why: because the Father sent Him and committed judgment to Him (v22). The honor is commanded, real, and total; and its stated ground is the Father's gift, not an underived equality. Honoring the Son rightly means honoring Him as the Sent One -- which honors the Sender most of all.

reason: Yeshua is the divine Son, the Word made flesh (John 1:14), the firstborn -- "a God" beside the God, sent, subject, and distinct. Rank ("greater than I"), initiative ("nothing of myself"), knowledge ("neither the Son") -- three attributes surrendered in the first person. Divine, yes; the Most High Himself, no. To confess the Son rightly is to confess the One who sent Him.

question: "Did Jesus die to satisfy God's wrath against sinners?"

sayings.quote: "...the Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a ransom for many."
sayings.expo: His own word for His own death: ransom -- lytron, the price that frees a captive or a slave. A ransom is aimed at the captor and the chains, not at the father of the captive. Nothing in the word involves wrath being absorbed; everything in it involves prisoners going free. He chose the vocabulary of liberation, not of punishment transferred.

sayings.quote: "But go ye and learn what that meaneth, I will have mercy, and not sacrifice..."
sayings.expo: Twice He sends the religious back to Hosea 6:6 -- "go and learn what it means." The Father's own stated preference is mercy over sacrificial payment. A theology in which the Father cannot forgive until a sacrifice satisfies Him is the exact logic Christ twice corrected. He would not quote "I desire mercy, not sacrifice" to describe a Father who desired the sacrifice of His Son before mercy became possible.

sayings.quote: "For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son..."
sayings.expo: Watch the order of events: the love comes first, the giving flows from it. The Father's love is the cause of the cross, not its purchased result. Penal substitution quietly reverses the verse -- as if the giving of the Son produced the love-warranted forgiveness. Christ says the Father so loved that He gave; He was never the obstacle the cross had to overcome.

reason: "God was IN Christ, reconciling the world unto himself" (2 Cor 5:19) -- the Father is the loving reconciler, not the angry party appeased. Wrath-satisfaction makes mercy a transaction and splits God against Himself: the Father demanding what the Son said He does not desire. The cross reveals love already given, pays the ransom that breaks sin and death's grip, and frees the captives -- that is what Christ said He came to do.

question: "Why is Christianity right and every other religion wrong?"

sayings.quote: "I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me."
sayings.expo: Not "a way" but "the way" -- and He closes the loophole Himself: "no man... but by me." Whatever one decides about this claim, it cannot be filed under "all paths are equal"; it is either true or false. Christ did not leave the all-mountain-paths option open -- the pluralist must first flatly contradict Him to include Him.

sayings.quote: "...neither knoweth any man the Father, save the Son, and he to whomsoever the Son will reveal him."
sayings.expo: The claim beneath the claim: the Father is known by revelation through the Son, not discovered by human climbing. Religions are man reaching up -- guesses, glimpses, fragments; this is God reaching down. That is why the ways are not interchangeable: only one of them claims, and offers evidence, that the Father Himself stepped into it.

sayings.quote: "Enter ye in at the strait gate... because strait is the gate, and narrow is the way, which leadeth unto life, and few there be that find it."
sayings.expo: He predicted the unpopularity of the claim: the true way is narrow and few find it, while the broad, comfortable road is crowded. So "most people believe otherwise" is not evidence against the way -- by His own words, the majority's road is precisely the one to question. Popularity was never the test; the gate was.

reason: Truth is exclusive by nature -- two and two are four, not five, and saying so is not bigotry. Claims that deny each other's core cannot all be true at once. The test is not which faith is nicest but which is TRUE -- which reveals the real Father. Other paths may hold fragments of light; the Son alone reveals Him. Exclusivity is a claim to weigh with evidence, not an insult to apologize for.

question: "Hasn't science -- evolution, the Big Bang -- disproved God and Genesis?"

sayings.quote: "But from the beginning of the creation God made them male and female."
sayings.expo: Asked about divorce, He answers from Genesis as fact: there was a beginning, it was a creation, and God made. Christ -- the one voice in history with standing to correct Genesis if it were myth -- instead built moral teaching on it. Whoever claims science retired the Creator must first claim Christ was wrong about where everything came from.

sayings.quote: "Have ye not read, that he which made them at the beginning made them male and female...?"
sayings.expo: The same ground, sharpened into a challenge: have ye not read? He treats the Genesis account as readable, public, and settled -- the thing his questioners should already know. He does not soften it into metaphor under pressure; He appeals to it as the record of what "he which made them" actually did.

sayings.quote: "...your heavenly Father feedeth them... Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow."
sayings.expo: Christ points at nature itself -- birds fed, lilies clothed -- as ongoing evidence of the Father's active care. In His teaching, studying how things grow is not a rival to faith; it is an invitation to it ("consider" -- katamathete, study closely). The book of nature and the book of Scripture have one Author; reading one closely was never supposed to close the other.

reason: Science studies mechanism -- "how," never "who" or "why." A universe with a beginning, finely tuned constants, and information written into life points toward a Mind, not away from one. Genesis tells the WHO and the WHY in the language of its hearers; it does not compete with a lab manual. "The heavens declare the glory of God" (Ps 19:1) -- the more we learn of them, the more there is to declare.

question: "What about all the hypocrites in the church?"

sayings.quote: "Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites!"
sayings.ref: Matt 23:13 -- eight times in one chapter
sayings.expo: No skeptic has ever denounced religious hypocrisy as fiercely as Christ did -- eight woes in a single spoken judgment, delivered to the most respected religious men of His nation, to their faces. "Hypocrite" (hypokritēs) is His word -- the stage-actor, the mask-wearer. The objector's outrage at hypocrisy is not a case against Christ; it is agreement with Him.

sayings.quote: "...first cast out the beam out of thine own eye; and then shalt thou see clearly to cast out the mote out of thy brother's eye."
sayings.expo: And the word is turned on the one pointing: first the beam in your own eye. The demand for integrity cuts everyone, including the critic cataloguing other people's failures. He does not excuse the church's sins -- He forbids using them as a mirror-avoidance device.

sayings.quote: "Not every one that saith unto me, Lord, Lord, shall enter into the kingdom of heaven... then will I profess unto them, I never knew you."
sayings.expo: Christ predicted the counterfeits by name: people who say "Lord, Lord," do works in His name -- and whom He never knew. The existence of false and failed Christians is not a hole in His teaching; it is a fulfilled forecast of it. He told us His name would be worn by people who do not belong to Him, and told us how He will answer them.

reason: Hypocrites prove the standard; they do not disprove it -- a counterfeit proves real gold exists. Judge the Physician by His own life and words, not by the sick still in His waiting room. The failures of men who wear His name no more disprove Him than forged banknotes disprove the mint. And the honest question is not "why are they hypocrites?" but "am I willing to be true?"

question: "Isn't faith just believing without evidence -- a crutch for the weak?"

sayings.quote: "Reach hither thy finger, and behold my hands; and reach hither thy hand, and thrust it into my side: and be not faithless, but believing."

question: "If God is sovereign and predestines everything, how can we have free will -- and how is judgment fair?"

sayings.quote: "O Jerusalem, Jerusalem... how often would I have gathered thy children together, even as a hen gathereth her chickens under her wings, and ye would not!"

Christ says His desire to gather them was real and repeated ("how often"), and the refusal was genuinely theirs. sayings.quote: "Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up... he spake of the temple of his body."
sayings.expo: The claim was made in advance, in public, to His enemies -- early enough that it was quoted (garbled) at His trial (Matt 26:61) and mocked at the cross. A legend accretes after the fact; a falsifiable public prediction is the opposite of legend. He staked the verdict on a date: three days. Everyone knew the deadline -- which is why the tomb was sealed and guarded (Matt 27:63-66: "after three days I will rise again," His enemies quoting Him).

sayings.quote: "I lay down my life, that I might take it again. No man taketh it from me... I have power to lay it down, and I have power to take it again."
sayings.expo: He framed His death, before it happened, as voluntary and reversible -- a laying down with authority (exousia) to take up. This rules out the "tragic martyr whose followers coped with visions" reconstruction: the man himself declared the plan, including the return leg. The skeptic must explain why a failed movement invented a prediction their leader had staked and -- on their theory -- lost.

question: "What about the Old Testament's violence -- didn't God command genocide?"

sayings.quote: "Ye know not what manner of spirit ye are of. For the Son of man is not come to destroy men's lives, but to save them."

Here is the Son, the exact image of the Father's heart, ruling on the use of divine violence by men: not to destroy, but to save. sayings.expo: Enemy-love is commanded as the family likeness -- "that ye may be the children of your Father." question: "Doesn't the Bible condone slavery?"

sayings.quote: "Therefore all things whatsoever ye would that men should do to you, do ye even so to them: for this is the law and the prophets."
sayings.expo: The golden rule is not one command among many -- He says it is the law and the prophets, the summary key to all of it. No man would be owned; therefore no man may own. Christ planted a principle that makes slaveholding self-condemning to anyone who applies it honestly -- which is exactly how the abolitionists, Bible in hand, argued it.

sayings.quote: "...whosoever will be great among you, shall be your minister: and whosoever of you will be the chiefest, shall be servant of all. For even the Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister..."
sayings.expo: He inverts the master-slave pyramid at its apex: greatness is serving, and the Lord of all takes the slave's role (washing feet -- the slave's task -- John 13). A kingdom whose King serves cannot canonize masters. This is not a rule bolted onto an old order; it is a new order in which the old one cannot breathe.

sayings.quote: "...he hath sent me to preach deliverance to the captives... to set at liberty them that are bruised."

question: "Why pray if God already knows everything and has a plan?"

sayings.quote: "...your Father knoweth what things ye have need of, before ye ask him. After this manner therefore pray ye..."
sayings.expo: Christ states the objection's premise Himself -- the Father already knows -- and draws the opposite conclusion: therefore pray. So in His teaching, prayer was never information delivery; the knowing Father still wants the asking child. What the objection thinks kills prayer is, in His mouth, the reason it is safe: you pray to One who knew before you spoke.

sayings.quote: "Ask, and it shall be given you; seek, and ye shall find; knock, and it shall be opened unto you."
sayings.expo: Three imperatives with three promises -- and all three verbs are continuous in the Greek: keep asking, keep seeking, keep knocking. He binds real outcomes to real asking: "every one that asketh receiveth." The Father has sovereignly chosen asking as a channel through which He gives -- so the asking is not beside the plan; it is in it, the way sowing is in the harvest.

question: "What happens to those who never heard of Jesus? Are they condemned?"

sayings.quote: "And that servant, which knew his lord's will, and prepared not himself... shall be beaten with many stripes. But he that knew not... shall be beaten with few stripes. For unto whomsoever much is given, of him shall be much required."
sayings.expo: Christ Himself scales judgment to light received: the one who "knew not" is judged differently from the one who knew. Responsibility tracks revelation -- His principle, stated as law. The objection's picture (identical condemnation regardless of knowledge) is precisely what this saying forbids. question: "Doesn't the Bible demean women?"

sayings.quote: "...Mary hath chosen that good part, which shall not be taken away from her."
sayings.expo: Mary was sitting at His feet -- the technical posture of a rabbinic disciple (Paul "at the feet of Gamaliel," Acts 22:3), a place no rabbi of the age gave a woman. Martha appealed to the custom (send her back to the kitchen); Christ overruled the custom and ratified the woman's place as disciple -- "it shall not be taken away from her." In one sentence, the door the culture closed, He fixed open.

sayings.quote: "...ought not this woman, being a daughter of Abraham... be loosed from this bond on the sabbath day?"
sayings.expo: To a bent-over woman the synagogue ruler saw as an interruption, Christ gives a title almost unheard in the literature of the era: "daughter of Abraham." Sons of Abraham was common coin; He mints the feminine deliberately, granting her the full covenant dignity the phrase carries -- and heals her over the official's objection. He does not merely include women; He names their standing out loud in public.

question: "If everything needs a creator -- then who made God?"

sayings.quote: "For as the Father hath life in himself; so hath he given to the Son to have life in himself."
sayings.expo: "Life in himself" -- underived, self-existent life -- is Scripture's own name for what the Father is: the one whose existence is not received from anything. And the sentence's grammar carries the theology: the Father has it; the Son is given it. Everything else -- the Son included, by gift -- receives; the Father alone simply is. The question "who made God?" asks who gave life to the One whose very definition is life ungiven.

sayings.quote: "God is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth."
sayings.expo: God is spirit -- not a body, not an object in the universe, not one more item in the chain of physical causes. "Who made X?" is a question for things inside the caused order of matter, energy, space, and time. Christ locates the Father outside that category entirely; asking what caused Him is asking what is north of the North Pole -- the question malfunctions, not the answer.

sayings.quote: "I am the God of Abraham... God is not the God of the dead, but of the living."
sayings.expo: Christ builds an argument on the living permanence of God: the I AM (quoting Exodus 3's self-name, "I AM THAT I AM") -- present tense across centuries, the One whose being does not pass. The name God gives Himself is not "I was made" but "I AM": existence itself, underived, the ground on which everything made stands. Christ treats that tense as strong enough to prove the resurrection from.

reason: The argument was never "everything needs a cause" -- it is "everything that begins needs a cause." The universe began (the objector's own cosmology says so): it therefore needs a cause. God did not begin; He needs none -- that is not special pleading but the very definition the case arrives at, since an infinite regress of caused causes explains nothing (a chain of borrowed lamps with no lamp that owns its light lights nothing). Something must have life in itself; the only question is whether that something is mindless or the living Father -- and mindless "just-exists" matter must then have produced minds, morals, and mathematics from nothing but itself.

question: "Hasn't the Bible been changed and corrupted over the centuries -- books picked by councils?"

sayings.quote: "...Till heaven and earth pass, one jot or one tittle shall in no wise pass from the law, till all be fulfilled."
sayings.expo: A jot is yod, the smallest Hebrew letter; a tittle is the pen-stroke distinguishing one letter from another. Christ vouches for preservation down to the stroke level -- and He said it holding copies of copies, a millennium and a half downstream from Moses. He did not treat hand-copying as garbling; He treated the scrolls in the synagogues as the word that would not pass. The Dead Sea Scrolls later tested exactly that claim: a thousand years older than our previous Hebrew copies -- and Isaiah read the same.

sayings.quote: "Heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away."
sayings.expo: A prediction, on the record, made by a wandering teacher with no scriptorium: His words would outlast the cosmos. Two thousand years on, His sayings are the most-copied, most-translated, most-scrutinized sentences in existence -- preserved in thousands of manuscripts beginning within living memory of the events (the John fragment P52, ~125 AD). The claim was falsifiable for twenty centuries; it has only compounded.

sayings.quote: "...the Comforter, which is the Holy Ghost... shall teach you all things, and bring all things to your remembrance, whatsoever I have said unto you."
sayings.expo: Christ pre-authorized the apostolic record: the Spirit would bring His words to the witnesses' remembrance. The Gospels are that promise executed -- eyewitness memory, Spirit-carried, written down while hostile witnesses still lived to contradict them. The books were not made authoritative by a later vote; they carried the authority of this commission from the day they were penned, and the assemblies recognized what they had received.

reason: Get the history straight: Nicaea (325) debated the Son's status and set no canon -- no council "picked the books" there; the lists (like Athanasius's, 367) recognized what the assemblies had read as apostolic for generations. The manuscript evidence is an embarrassment of riches -- 5,800+ Greek NT manuscripts against a handful for any other ancient text -- and the "telephone game" fails as an analogy: copying was written, parallel, and checkable across independent streams, so errors in one line are corrected by the others. The real variants are spelling and word order; no doctrine hangs on any of them. The text is the best-attested artifact of the ancient world -- by far.

question: "If God exists, why doesn't He just show Himself?"

sayings.quote: "...he that hath seen me hath seen the Father..."
sayings.expo: The claim of the faith is not that God stayed hidden -- it is that He showed Himself: walked, taught, healed, wept, was touched, and was seen by thousands. Philip asked the objector's exact question ("shew us the Father") and this was the answer. The demand "God should show up in person" has been met; the question is what the generation that saw Him did with it -- and what we do with their testimony.

sayings.quote: "If they hear not Moses and the prophets, neither will they be persuaded, though one rose from the dead."
sayings.expo: Christ's own verdict on the "more spectacle would convince me" theory -- and He proved it twice: He raised a Lazarus, and the officials plotted to kill Lazarus too (John 12:10); He rose Himself, and the guards' report was bought off (Matt 28:12-15). Evidence compels only the willing. A sky-writing God would not convert the unwilling; He would merely relocate their explanation (mass delusion, alien optics -- the modern reflex proves the point). The block is not optical; it is volitional.

sayings.quote: "If any man will do his will, he shall know of the doctrine, whether it be of God..." -- and: "Blessed are the pure in heart: for they shall see God."
sayings.expo: He publishes the protocol for seeing: willingness first, then knowing; purity of heart, then sight. Knowing God is not like reading a billboard -- it is like knowing a person, and persons are known through trust, approach, and time. God has calibrated His visibility for relationship, not coercion: light enough for any seeker to find, shadow enough that no rebel is dragged in by the eyes. He wants sons, not subjects compelled by spectacle.

reason: The Father is not hiding: the heavens declare Him (Ps 19:1), conscience carries His law, He is "not far from every one of us" (Acts 17:27), He came in the Son, and He gives the Holy Spirit to them that ask (Luke 11:13) -- asked aloud, in private, persistently. That last is the standing offer the objection never tests: the evidence God promises is first-person, and the experiment is prayer. A man who will not perform the experiment cannot cite the absence of its result. Seek, and ye shall find (Matt 7:7) -- the finding was always downstream of the seeking.

question: "How can a modern person believe in miracles?"

sayings.quote: "If I do not the works of my Father, believe me not. But if I do, though ye believe not me, believe the works..."
sayings.expo: Christ submits His claims to an evidence test He proposes Himself: don't take my word -- check the works. That is the opposite of "believe blindly"; it is an invitation to verification, issued to hostile examiners. A faith whose founder says believe me not unless the evidence stands is not the pre-scientific credulity the objection imagines.

sayings.quote: "Go and shew John again those things which ye do hear and see: The blind receive their sight, and the lame walk, the lepers are cleansed, and the deaf hear..."
sayings.expo: When John the Baptist doubted from prison, Christ sent data, not scolding: things "ye do hear and see" -- public, plural, checkable healings, of conditions (born blind, leprous, dead) that no placebo touches. The miracles were performed before crowds and enemies; the Pharisees' own councils never denied the works -- they attributed them elsewhere (Matt 12:24), which concedes the events.

sayings.quote: "...This is an evil generation: they seek a sign; and there shall no sign be given it, but the sign of Jonas."
sayings.expo: And yet He refused signs-on-demand for spectacle. Miracles in His hands are purposeful attestation, not circus performance -- clustered at revelation's hinge-points, capped by the one sign He staked everything on: as Jonah, three days and out. He would not entertain; He would rise. That discipline is itself evidence -- inventors of wonder-tales multiply wonders; the record shows restraint.

reason: A miracle is not a violation of nature but an act of nature's Author within it -- and whether one occurred is a question of testimony and evidence, exactly like any historical event. The circle in the objection: "miracles don't happen" is assumed in order to dismiss every report that they did -- the conclusion doing duty as the filter. If the Father exists, miracles are possible; whether they are actual is settled by witnesses -- and for the sign of Jonah the witnesses were many, hostile-checked, and unbreakable under death.

question: "Didn't Jesus never actually claim to be the Messiah or the Son of God?"

sayings.quote: "Again the high priest asked him... Art thou the Christ, the Son of the Blessed? And Jesus said, I am: and ye shall see the Son of man sitting on the right hand of power..."
sayings.expo: Under oath, at trial, with His life on the line -- the one moment silence would have saved Him -- He answers the exact question directly: "I am." The Christ, the Son of the Blessed. And this is Mark, the earliest and plainest Gospel, not John. The claim cost Him His life on the spot ("ye have heard the blasphemy"); no later church needed to invent what the court convicted Him for.

sayings.quote: "The woman saith... I know that Messias cometh... Jesus saith unto her, I that speak unto thee am he."
sayings.expo: His most explicit Messiah-claim was made privately, to a Samaritan woman -- the least strategic audience imaginable for an invented legend, and exactly the audience a real man avoiding premature arrest might trust. The pattern (guarded in Judea, open in Samaria, confessed at trial) is the behavior of a real claimant managing a real danger -- not a script.

sayings.quote: "...Whom say ye that I am? And Simon Peter answered... Thou art the Christ, the Son of the living God. And Jesus answered... flesh and blood hath not revealed it unto thee, but my Father which is in heaven."
sayings.expo: He solicits the confession ("whom say ye...?"), then blesses it as revelation from the Father -- the strongest possible ratification. A teacher who thought "Christ, Son of the living God" was a mistake corrects it; He canonized it. Even His favored title "Son of man" is itself a claim -- Daniel 7's figure who comes with clouds and receives an everlasting kingdom, which is precisely how He used it at trial.

reason: Yeshua claimed to be exactly what Tav'iel confesses: the Christ, the Son of the living God, sent by the Father -- and He accepted worship-honor as the Sent One (John 5:23). What He did not claim is the later formula: co-equality with the Father He called "the only true God" (John 17:3) and "greater than I" (John 14:28). So both camps err: the skeptic erases claims Mark records under oath; the tradition inflates them past the Son's own words. The record itself -- Messiah, Son, sent, subordinate -- is the true confession.

question: "I prayed and nothing happened -- why doesn't God answer prayer?"

sayings.quote: "O my Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me: nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt."
sayings.expo: The most fervent prayer ever prayed -- sweat like blood -- and the cup did not pass. Christ Himself experienced "no" as the Father's answer, and had already taught us to pray "thy will be done" (Matt 6:10) -- the clause the objection calls an excuse is the petition's own hinge, prayed first by Him. Prayer, in His practice, was never a vending machine that failed; it was a Son's surrender that triumphed -- the "no" in the garden carried the ransom of the world.

sayings.quote: "If a son shall ask bread of any of you that is a father, will he give him a stone?... how much more shall your heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to them that ask him?"
sayings.expo: He anchors prayer in fatherhood, not mechanics: a father gives -- but gives good gifts, which means he also refuses the serpent his child mistakes for a fish. And notice what the escalation lands on: the promised certain answer is the Holy Spirit -- the gift the Father never refuses to the asker. Many prayers aim at circumstances; the guaranteed grant is God Himself. That is not a lowered target; it is the one that changes the asker.

sayings.quote: "...My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness." -- the risen Christ, refusing Paul's thrice-made request.
sayings.expo: A recorded, explicit divine "no" -- with the reason attached. The thorn stayed; the grace came; the strength arrived through the unremoved weakness. So Scripture itself documents unanswered petition and interprets it: some things God will not take away because of what He intends to give through them. The faith does not hide its "no"s -- it frames them, from the garden to the thorn.

reason: Prayer is not a slot machine to be audited; it is a Father listened to and answered as a Father -- yes, no, and not-yet are all answers, as every child of a good parent knows. The studies measure prayer as incantation over strangers, which is precisely what Christ said it isn't. Ask rightly and the certainties are real: the Holy Spirit to them that ask (Luke 11:13), wisdom, forgiveness sought with a whole heart -- and for the rest, the Gethsemane order stands: honest desire, poured out, surrendered -- "nevertheless." The prayer that cannot "fail" is the one He taught, because its center is the Father's will, not the wish list.

question: "Christians pick and choose -- you quote Leviticus but eat shellfish. Why keep some laws and not others?"

sayings.quote: "Think not that I am come to destroy the law, or the prophets: I am not come to destroy, but to fulfil."
sayings.expo: His own category: fulfil -- plērōsai, to fill full, to bring to its intended completion. Not abolition, not arbitrary selection: completion. A promissory note is not "cherry-picked" when it is paid; the sacrificial and ceremonial shadows (temple, offerings, cleanness) reached their substance in the ransom He gave. What a law was for determines what fulfilment does to it -- and He claimed to be what the whole fabric was for.

sayings.quote: "...ye pay tithe of mint and anise and cummin, and have omitted the weightier matters of the law, judgment, mercy, and faith: these ought ye to have done, and not to leave the other undone."
sayings.expo: Christ Himself ranks within the law -- "weightier matters" -- while forbidding the false dilemma ("and not to leave the other undone"). So distinguishing within the law is not cherry-picking; it is His hermeneutic. The law was never a flat list; it had a spine (justice, mercy, faith) and members serving the spine. Reading it that way is obedience to its Giver's own instruction.

sayings.quote: "Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart... Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself. On these two commandments hang all the law and the prophets."
sayings.expo: The organizing key, from His mouth: everything hangs from two loves. Laws are kept according to what they hang from -- the moral law (the Ten Words) articulates the two loves permanently; Israel's civil statutes applied them to one nation's courts; the ceremonial shadowed the Redeemer to come. One fabric, three threads, one test: what does this command serve, and how does its purpose stand now that He has come?

reason: The distinction is in the text, not invented over it: Israel's own law treated the Ten Words differently -- spoken by God's voice, written by His finger, placed inside the ark -- from the statutes and ordinances around them. The dietary and ceremonial laws marked a nation as set apart and shadowed the cleansing to come; their purpose met its substance. The moral law -- the Ten, the two loves -- was never Israel's alone and never expired; Yeshua deepened it to the heart (Matt 5). So: shellfish, fulfilled sign; "thou shalt not steal," standing word. That is not a buffet; it is reading a covenant the way its Mediator read it.
argument:
Yeshua said, "Think not that I am come to destroy the law, or the prophets: I am not come to destroy, but to fulfil." (Matt 5:17). His own category: fulfil -- plērōsai, to fill full, to bring to its intended completion. Not abolition, not arbitrary selection: completion. A promissory note is not "cherry-picked" when it is paid; the sacrificial and ceremonial shadows (temple, offerings, cleanness) reached their substance in the ransom He gave. What a law was for determines what fulfilment does to it -- and He claimed to be what the whole fabric was for.

Yeshua said, "...ye pay tithe of mint and anise and cummin, and have omitted the weightier matters of the law, judgment, mercy, and faith: these ought ye to have done, and not to leave the other undone." (Matt 23:23). Christ Himself ranks within the law -- "weightier matters" -- while forbidding the false dilemma ("and not to leave the other undone"). So distinguishing within the law is not cherry-picking; it is His hermeneutic. The law was never a flat list; it had a spine (justice, mercy, faith) and members serving the spine. Reading it that way is obedience to its Giver's own instruction.

question: "What about homosexuality? Jesus never even mentioned it."

sayings.quote: "Have ye not read, that he which made them at the beginning made them male and female... For this cause shall a man leave father and mother, and shall cleave to his wife: and they twain shall be one flesh?"
sayings.expo: Asked about marriage, Christ answered with a definition, not a list of exclusions: from the beginning -- male and female -- man and wife -- one flesh. He grounded it in creation's design, before Moses, before culture. "He never mentioned it" mistakes silence about a term for silence about the substance: He defined the covenant positively, and a definition settles everything outside it without naming each thing. He also named the alternative He honored: some make themselves eunuchs for the kingdom (19:12) -- faithful marriage or consecrated singleness.

sayings.quote: "Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more."
sayings.expo: Before a woman taken in sexual sin, with the stone-holders circling, Christ does both things at once the modern debate splits apart: no condemnation -- and no blessing of the sin. He disarms the executioners ("he that is without sin among you..."), then speaks the call: go, and sin no more. Mercy without license; truth without a stone. Whoever quotes half this verse -- either half -- is not quoting Him.

sayings.expo: The saying most quoted at Christians is Christ's -- and it governs the manner, not the message: the beam comes out first so that "thou shalt see clearly" to help with the mote -- the goal is restored sight, not silence about motes. He forbids the contempt, the singling-out of one sin as though it were the unforgivable one, the crowd with stones. He never forbids calling His own definition His own definition.

question: "Does the Sabbath still matter -- and why do most churches keep Sunday?"

sayings.quote: "The sabbath was made for man, and not man for the sabbath: Therefore the Son of man is Lord also of the sabbath."
sayings.expo: Two anchors in one saying. "Made for man" -- anthrōpos, mankind -- reaching back to the making itself (Gen 2:2-3): a creation gift blessed before Sinai, before any Jew existed; not tribal law but human birthright. And "the Son of man is Lord of the sabbath" -- He claims the day as His own domain. A lord does not abolish his own estate; He rules it, and He spent His sabbaths freeing people (Luke 13:16) to show what the day is for.

sayings.quote: "And he came to Nazareth... and, as his custom was, he went into the synagogue on the sabbath day, and stood up for to read."
sayings.expo: His custom -- the settled habit of His life -- was the seventh-day assembly. Every recorded sabbath of His ministry is the seventh day; He corrected the day's abuses (the burdens rabbis had piled on) and never once its date. The disciples after the cross "rested the sabbath day according to the commandment" (Luke 23:56) -- Luke, writing decades later for a Gentile, still calls the seventh day "the commandment."

sayings.quote: "But pray ye that your flight be not in the winter, neither on the sabbath day."
sayings.expo: Speaking of a flight forty years future -- Jerusalem's fall in 70 AD -- He assumes His people will still be keeping the sabbath, and cares how it goes for them. A teacher who had scheduled the day's obsolescence at the resurrection would not pray-proof a sabbath four decades past it. His horizon has the day standing.

reason: The seventh day is the only commandment that begins "Remember" -- and it is the one most forgotten. It was blessed at creation (Gen 2:3), spoken by God's own voice at Sinai as the fourth of the Ten, kept by Yeshua as His custom, and guarded by His disciples after the cross. No verse moves it; the transfer to Sunday came by later custom and church authority, centuries on -- history its own advocates concede. The gift stands as made: a day the Maker blessed for man -- for rest, mercy, and the Father's presence -- and the Lord of it showed how it is kept: not as a cage, but as a liberation.

question: "The church just wants your money -- look at the tithing pressure and the prosperity preachers."

sayings.quote: "...freely ye have received, freely give."
sayings.expo: His commissioning charge to the first preachers -- with "provide neither gold, nor silver, nor brass in your purses" right behind it (10:9). The gospel's price, set by its Owner: free. Whoever sells what Christ commanded be given has broken the founding charter of the ministry in the act of exercising it. The objection's outrage at merchandised religion is not modern skepticism; it is Matthew 10.

sayings.quote: "...make not my Father's house an house of merchandise." -- with a whip of cords, overturning the money-changers' tables.
sayings.expo: The one scene of Christ's physical anger in all four Gospels -- and its target is commerce wearing worship's clothes. He did it twice (again in Matt 21:13: "a den of thieves"). The men monetizing the temple courts were the prosperity preachers of their day, and His verdict on them is the whip and the overturned table. No skeptic has ever judged religious profiteering more violently than its Lord did.

sayings.quote: "No man can serve two masters... Ye cannot serve God and mammon."
sayings.expo: Not "should not" -- cannot: the two masterships are mutually exclusive by nature. A gospel that promises mammon as the reward for serving God has fused what Christ declared unfusable; it is not a distortion of His teaching but its inversion. He was poor ("the Son of man hath not where to lay his head," Matt 8:20), praised the widow's two mites over the rich men's gifts (Luke 21:2-4), and warned that riches choke the word (Matt 13:22).

reason: The objection is aimed at men Christ condemned before the objector was born -- fire it at them, and He is on your side of the line. Real giving in His teaching is free, secret ("let not thy left hand know," Matt 6:3), aimed at the poor, and never a lever on God: the Father is not a slot machine, and "seed money" doctrine is the money-changers' table rebuilt in a broadcast studio. Judge the faith by its Founder -- who owned nothing, charged nothing, and drove the merchandisers out -- and the scandal of the profiteers becomes evidence for His standard, not against it.

question: "What about reincarnation and near-death experiences -- don't they show the Bible has it wrong?"

sayings.quote: "Marvel not at this: for the hour is coming, in the which all that are in the graves shall hear his voice, and shall come forth..."
sayings.expo: Christ's map of what follows death is resurrection, not recycling: the dead are "in the graves," they wait, and at His voice they come forth -- the same persons, raised, to judgment or life. Reincarnation erases the person to reuse the soul-stuff; resurrection restores the person. The two are not variants of one hope; they are opposite verdicts on whether you -- this name, this story -- matter enough to be kept.

sayings.quote: "I am the resurrection, and the life: he that believeth in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live..."
sayings.expo: Spoken at a tomb, to a grieving sister -- and then demonstrated on the spot: "Lazarus, come forth" (11:43). Christ did not theorize about the afterlife; He reversed a death in public, before hostile witnesses, as the sign of His claim. Lazarus did not return as another creature with dim memories; he walked out as Lazarus. The one man in history with authority over the grave described what it holds -- sleepers awaiting His voice (11:11) -- and proved He could call them.

sayings.quote: "I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob... God is not the God of the dead, but of the living."
sayings.expo: Against the Sadducees -- that age's deniers of any life to come -- Christ argues from the covenant name: the Father remains their God, so Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob remain themselves in His keeping, secured for the resurrection. Identity is preserved, not dissolved into another birth. The dead a person "remembers being" would have to still be that person -- which is exactly the continuity reincarnation denies and resurrection keeps.

reason: Weigh the evidence honestly: past-life memories cluster where reincarnation is already taught, bloom under hypnosis (a state that manufactures confident false memory), and their checkable details fail more than they land. NDEs are experiences of the dying, not the dead -- the brain's borderland, shaped by the traveler's expectations -- and where they contradict each other across cultures they cannot all be reports of one geography. Christ's account asks no such patchwork: one life ("it is appointed unto men once to die"), a keeping Father, a waking at His voice. And its proof is not a tunnel of light but an opened tomb with witnesses.

question: "Isn't Jesus just a copy of pagan myths -- Horus, Mithras, the dying-and-rising gods?"

sayings.quote: "...all things must be fulfilled, which were written in the law of Moses, and in the prophets, and in the psalms, concerning me."
sayings.expo: Christ names His own source-tradition, explicitly and exhaustively: Moses, the prophets, the psalms -- the Hebrew Scriptures, centuries of them, publicly datable, in hand long before He was born. His frame of reference is Isaiah 53 and Psalm 22, not Egypt or Persia. The story's soil is not a mystery: He plowed it in front of His disciples, text by text, on the Emmaus road.

sayings.quote: "For had ye believed Moses, ye would have believed me: for he wrote of me."
sayings.expo: He stakes His identity on documents His opponents owned -- "he wrote of me." That is a checkable claim inside a literate covenant community obsessed with those very scrolls; it invites the audit. Myth-figures are congealed from anonymous retellings; Christ points at named books on His hearers' shelves and says: read them, I am there. The direction of dependence is declared, public, and falsifiable.

sayings.quote: "...Ought not Christ to have suffered these things, and to enter into his glory?" -- "O fools, and slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken."
sayings.expo: Note what He must argue for: a suffering, dying Messiah was so alien to every expectation -- Jewish and pagan alike -- that His own disciples couldn't believe it until He walked them through the prophets. Nobody's mythology delivered a crucified god as its hero; crucifixion was the empire's obscenity ("foolishness to the Greeks"). A borrowed savior would have been built to flatter the audience. This one scandalized everyone -- the signature of an unwelcome fact, not a marketed myth.

reason: Check the actual sources and the parallels evaporate: Horus was not born of a virgin (Isis conceived by the reassembled Osiris), had no twelve, no crucifixion, no resurrection after three days; Mithras was born from a rock, and the Roman Mithras-cult's evidence post-dates Christianity -- where there was borrowing, it ran the other way. December 25 appears in no Gospel at all -- it is a later church custom, not a claim of the text. The "dying-rising god" category was largely manufactured by nineteenth-century comparativists rounding every harvest myth up to a resurrection. Yeshua enters history as a datable man, under a datable governor, fulfilling datable Scriptures -- myth has no crucifixion under Pontius Pilate.

question: "Hasn't religion caused most of the world's wars and violence?"

sayings.quote: "Put up again thy sword into his place: for all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword."
sayings.expo: Spoken at His own arrest, to a disciple defending Him -- the one cause that might justify a blade, and He forbids it, heals the wound (Luke 22:51), and states the law of the blade: it consumes its wielders. Christ's last free act before the cross was to disarm His church. Every later crusader had to sheathe this verse to draw his sword.

sayings.quote: "Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God."
sayings.expo: In His kingdom's constitution, the family resemblance of God's children is making peace -- not winning wars. Paired with "love your enemies" (5:44), it defines the community He founded: one that absorbs violence rather than deals it. For its first three centuries that is what the church was known for -- dying in arenas, not killing in armies. The deviation came with empire, and it deviated from this text.

sayings.quote: "The kings of the Gentiles exercise lordship over them... But ye shall not be so..."
sayings.expo: The night before His death He drew the line that indicts every state-church bloodletting since: Gentile power rules by domination -- "ye shall not be so." When men killed with cross-painted shields, they were being exactly what He forbade: kings of the Gentiles in borrowed vestments. The corruption of the best is the worst -- but it is a corruption, measurable against the explicit command it defied.

reason: Now the ledger, honestly: the standard survey of history's wars (the Encyclopedia of Wars, 1,763 catalogued) classes under seven percent as religious -- land, dynasty, and plunder dwarf creed. And the twentieth century ran the objection's own experiment: regimes that abolished God -- Stalin, Mao, the Khmer Rouge -- out-killed all the religious wars of history combined, in one lifetime. Violence is not a religion problem; it is a human problem, and it wears whatever coat the age respects -- a cross once, a flag or a five-year plan since. The one force that has no alibi is the actual teaching of the actual Christ: sword down, enemies loved, peacemakers blessed.

question: "Isn't God just a 'God of the gaps' -- shrinking as science explains more?"

sayings.quote: "Behold the fowls of the air... your heavenly Father feedeth them... Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow."
sayings.expo: Christ locates the Father in the explained, not the unexplained: birds feeding and lilies growing are utterly ordinary processes -- seed, soil, season -- and He names them the Father's daily work. His God was never hiding in gaps; He is the one sustaining the regularities science describes. Explaining the mechanism more finely describes His working more finely.

sayings.quote: "My Father worketh hitherto, and I work."

question: "Is the Old Testament God different from the New Testament God?"

sayings.quote: "The Son can do nothing of himself, but what he seeth the Father do: for what things soever he doeth, these also doeth the Son likewise."
sayings.expo: Christ describes Himself as the Father's exact imitation -- everything He does is copied from what He sees the Father doing. So every healing, every embrace of a sinner, every tear was, by His own account, a portrait of the OT's God. If the Father were the thunder-god of the caricature, the Son mirroring Him would have looked like it.

sayings.quote: "Be ye therefore merciful, as your Father also is merciful."

sayings.quote: "The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he hath anointed me to preach the gospel to the poor..." -- reading Isaiah of Himself.
sayings.expo: His ministry's opening act: unrolling an OT scroll and announcing "this day is this scripture fulfilled." Christ is the OT God's love made visible, on the OT God's schedule.

question: "Why the cross at all? Couldn't God just forgive?"

sayings.quote: "Thinkest thou that I cannot now pray to my Father, and he shall presently give me more than twelve legions of angels? But how then shall the scriptures be fulfilled, that thus it must be?"
sayings.expo: Christ affirms the objection's premise -- escape was available, omnipotence stood ready -- and overrides it with purpose: thus it must be. The cross was not a constraint on God's power but a choice of God's wisdom; the "must" is the logic of a rescue plan written in the prophets, not a ransom note God was forced to pay.

sayings.quote: "Verily, verily, I say unto you, Except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die, it abideth alone: but if it die, it bringeth forth much fruit."
sayings.expo: His own explanation of why dying was the way: some things are only reachable through death -- as a seed's life multiplies only by burial. Mere pardon leaves the captive pardoned and still captive; death-and-rising breaks the captor's grip and plants a new humanity. Forgiveness erases the record; the cross-and-resurrection changes the prisoner.

sayings.quote: "And as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of man be lifted up: That whosoever believeth in him should not perish..."
sayings.expo: His chosen picture is the bronze serpent -- a cure displayed, not a payment rendered: the bitten looked and lived. The lifting up is remedy and revelation -- the love of God made visible at maximum cost, sin's whole machinery (betrayal, injustice, cruelty) exhausted upon Him and answered with "Father, forgive them." One look at that, and the poison loses.

reason: God's forgiveness was never for sale -- He forgave freely all through the OT (Ps 103:3). The cross was not the price that made the Father willing; it was the willing Father's rescue: a ransom that frees captives from sin and death (Mark 10:45), death itself destroyed by being swallowed, love demonstrated beyond all argument (Rom 5:8). "Just forgive" heals the ledger and leaves the disease; the Father chose the cure -- costly to Him, free to us.

question: "Six days? A young earth? How can anyone read Genesis 1 literally?"

sayings.quote: "But from the beginning of the creation God made them male and female."
sayings.expo: Mankind is placed "from the beginning of the creation" -- not fourteen billion years after it. Christ's timeline has humanity at creation's start, which is Genesis read plainly and the long chronology read not at all. Whatever one does with the ages, one must first deal with the Author's Son summarizing His Father's book this way.

sayings.quote: "For as in the days that were before the flood they were eating and drinking, marrying... until the day that Noe entered into the ark."
sayings.expo: He handles Genesis' primeval chapters as history with dates and a door -- real days, real meals, a real ark entered on a real day. Christ never signals "now I'm using poetry"; He builds His end-times teaching on the flood's factuality. The genre call the objection needs ("it's all metaphor") is a call He conspicuously never made.

sayings.quote: "...the blood of all the prophets... from the blood of Abel unto the blood of Zacharias..."
sayings.expo: Christ's martyr-roll runs in one unbroken line from Abel -- Adam's son, the first generation -- to His own century, "required of this generation." The genealogy is short, continuous, and real to Him: Eden's family and Jerusalem's stand in the same courtroom. A mankind hundreds of millennia old with mythical first chapters cannot produce this sentence.

reason: The text says evening and morning, numbered days, and genealogies with lifespans -- it reads as record, and its Lord read it so. The ages, by contrast, are inference: measured rates assumed constant across an unobserved past, models revised every generation (and a Maker who made trees bearing fruit and light already arriving made a world with functional maturity from day one). Hold the Word steady and the models loosely -- it has outlasted every cosmology that was "settled" before this one, from eternal-universe Aristotle to steady-state, and it will outlast the next.

question: "Hasn't the church always fought science? Remember Galileo."

sayings.quote: "And ye shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free."
sayings.expo: Christ binds freedom to knowing truth -- an epistemology of liberation. A faith whose founder says truth frees cannot coherently fear inquiry; every honest instrument is on its side. Whenever churchmen suppressed honest findings, they were disobeying this verse, not applying it.

sayings.quote: "But he that doeth truth cometh to the light, that his deeds may be made manifest..."
sayings.expo: Truth-doers come toward the light and welcome examination -- Christ's definition of integrity is manifestation, the laboratory's own ethic: publish, show, verify. Concealment and censorship belong, in His taxonomy, to the other column ("every one that doeth evil hateth the light"). The scientific virtues are Johannine virtues.

sayings.quote: "To this end was I born... that I should bear witness unto the truth. Every one that is of the truth heareth my voice."
sayings.expo: Before Rome's power, He defines His whole mission as witness to truth -- truth as allegiance, above institutions and their interests. The men who founded modern science took Him at His word: Kepler called astronomy "thinking God's thoughts after him"; Newton wrote more theology than physics; the law-governed cosmos they expected, they expected because a Lawgiver had spoken.

reason: Check the record: modern science was born in Christendom -- universities, Copernicus (a church canon), Kepler, Boyle, Faraday, Maxwell, Mendel (a friar), Lemaître (the Big Bang's father, a priest). When the institution fought discovery, it fought its own Lord's charter: the truth shall make you free.

question: "Is suicide unforgivable? What does God think of the mentally ill?"

sayings.quote: "A bruised reed shall he not break, and smoking flax shall he not quench, till he send forth judgment unto victory."
sayings.expo: The prophecy Matthew applies to Christ's manner: the bruised reed -- the person bent to breaking -- He will not snap; the smoking flax -- a wick down to its last ember of smoke -- He will not put out. His entire posture toward the barely-hanging-on is preservation. Whoever taught the despairing that God waits to damn them taught the opposite of this verse.

sayings.quote: "...he hath sent me to heal the brokenhearted..."
sayings.expo: In His mission statement, the brokenhearted are not a liability He tolerates but a commission He was sent for. Mental anguish is, in His economy, a wound to be healed -- never a verdict, never a shame. He handled the tormented of His day (the man among the tombs, cutting himself -- Mark 5) with deliverance and dignity: "sitting, and clothed, and in his right mind."

sayings.quote: "And I give unto them eternal life; and they shall never perish, neither shall any man pluck them out of my hand."
sayings.expo: The grip that keeps the sheep is His, not the sheep's -- and no one, He says, can pry it open. A believer's darkest hour, even a final one, does not overpower that hand; the Judge who holds them knows the illness, the medication, the chemistry, the despair -- everything a church tribunal never could. Judgment is scaled to light and capacity (Luke 12:48), and it is His alone.

reason: Scripture never says suicide is the unforgivable sin -- that sin is defined elsewhere and is something else entirely (Round 39). The old funeral-denial rules were men's, not the Word's. Depression is illness, not faithlessness: Elijah under the juniper asked to die and God sent food and sleep, not a rebuke (1 Kings 19). If the darkness is on you: the Father is not waiting to condemn you -- He is the one holding the wick; and He also works through help, doctors, and friends. Stay. Tell someone. The Man of sorrows is not ashamed of you.

question: "What did Jesus actually teach about divorce and remarriage?"

sayings.quote: "Moses because of the hardness of your hearts suffered you to put away your wives: but from the beginning it was not so."
sayings.expo: Two layers, both His: the design (from the beginning -- one flesh, lifelong) and the concession (Moses suffered it, for hardness). Divorce law existed to restrain sinners' damage -- Deut 24's certificate protected the woman from limbo -- not to bless the rupture. Christ restores the design without denying that law must deal with hardness.

sayings.quote: "...whosoever shall put away his wife, saving for the cause of fornication, causeth her to commit adultery..."
sayings.expo: He states an exception in the same breath as the rule -- porneia, sexual unfaithfulness, breaks the one-flesh bond He is protecting. So "Jesus banned divorce outright" is not what He said; He banned the casual, any-cause divorce the rabbis of Hillel's school were licensing (burnt dinner sufficed), while naming the betrayal that genuinely severs. And note who His rule defends: the discarded wife.

sayings.quote: "Thou hast well said, I have no husband: For thou hast had five husbands... Jesus saith unto her, I that speak unto thee am he."
sayings.expo: To a five-times-married woman at a well, Christ speaks truth without contempt -- and entrusts to her His plainest Messiah-declaration, making her a city's first evangelist. His standard is high and His mercy is higher; the divorced are not His castoffs but, in the record, among His first preachers.

reason: The teaching is neither trap nor dead letter: design honored, betrayal named as release, and the abandoned protected -- Paul adds desertion to the release grounds (1 Cor 7:15), and abuse is desertion of the covenant in all but address; the shepherds who chain the beaten to their beater serve hardness, not marriage. But the modern any-cause exit Christ confronted at Hillel's door He confronts at ours: covenants are not consumer goods. High view, real exceptions, mercy for the broken -- that is the actual teaching, and it works wherever it is actually tried.

question: "Why did God allow polygamy in the Bible?"

sayings.quote: "...he which made them at the beginning made them male and female... and they twain shall be one flesh."
sayings.expo: The arithmetic of the design is in the word twain: two become one -- not three, not seven hundred. Christ answers every marriage question by returning to the origin: one man, one woman, one flesh. Polygamy is not condemned by a proof-text; it is excluded by the equation.

sayings.quote: "...because of the hardness of your hearts... but from the beginning it was not so."
sayings.expo: Here is His stated principle for every tolerated deviation, divorce and polygamy alike: law managed hardness; the beginning holds the design. God regulating a practice (limiting kings' wives, protecting the less-loved wife's rights -- Deut 21:15-17) is damage control inside a hard-hearted age, not endorsement -- the same way a law regulating divorce never blessed it.

sayings.quote: "...he which made them at the beginning... What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder."
sayings.expo: "What God hath joined" -- the joining He owns is the two-into-one; the harems were man's joining, and Scripture audits them honestly: Sarah against Hagar, Leah weeping against Rachel, David's house on fire, Solomon's heart turned (1 Kings 11:3-4 states it as cause). The Bible reports its heroes' polygamy the way it reports their lies -- with the wreckage attached.

reason: Description is not prescription: the Book that records the patriarchs' plural marriages also records, without exception, the misery inside them -- rivalry, favoritism, and dynastic blood. The law fenced the practice (a king "shall not multiply wives," Deut 17:17 -- the verse Solomon shattered) and defended its victims; the prophets' image of God's own covenant is one Husband, one bride; and the Son closed the question by reopening Eden. "Biblical marriage" means marriage as the Bible's God designed and the Bible's Christ defined it -- the failures in between are the case study, not the standard.

question: "What is the unforgivable sin -- and have I committed it?"

sayings.quote: "All manner of sin and blasphemy shall be forgiven unto men: but the blasphemy against the Holy Ghost shall not be forgiven..."
sayings.expo: Start where He starts: all manner of sin and blasphemy forgivable -- murder, adultery, even words against the Son Himself (v32). The saying is a blazing declaration of forgiveness's reach with one boundary -- so the fearful reader has the emphasis backwards. Whatever the boundary is, the field inside it is "all manner."

sayings.quote: "...Because they said, He hath an unclean spirit."
sayings.expo: Mark supplies the context clause the terror forgets: Christ said it because the Pharisees, seeing the Spirit's own liberating work with their eyes, called it Satan's. That is the sin: not a slipped word, but the settled, eyes-open verdict that calls the Spirit's light darkness -- slamming, from the inside, the only door forgiveness comes through. It is not an accident one commits; it is a heart one becomes.

question: "Why do children die -- and where do they go?"

sayings.quote: "Suffer little children, and forbid them not, to come unto me: for of such is the kingdom of heaven."
sayings.expo: The disciples treated children as interruptions; Christ was much displeased (Mark 10:14) and declared the kingdom theirs -- "of such is the kingdom." Children are not marginal candidates awaiting qualification; they are the kingdom's native citizens, the model the rest of us must convert to (Matt 18:3). Whatever theology damns an infant has reversed its Lord.

sayings.quote: "Take heed that ye despise not one of these little ones; for I say unto you, That in heaven their angels do always behold the face of my Father."
sayings.expo: The little ones have standing agents at the highest court -- "always behold the face of my Father": unbroken access, permanent representation. No child dies unnoticed or unattended; the smallest griefs on earth are presented perpetually at the throne. This is Christ's own picture of how heaven is organized around children.

sayings.quote: "Even so it is not the will of your Father which is in heaven, that one of these little ones should perish."
sayings.expo: Stated flatly: their perishing is not the Father's will. Death in a children's ward is the enemy's work in a war-torn creation ("an enemy hath done this," Matt 13:28) -- the very thing Christ came to destroy, weeping at a tomb He was about to empty (John 11:35). God's will concerning children has one recorded direction: that they be brought to Him and kept.

reason: Where do they go? Into the will just quoted. Judgment is scaled to light (Luke 12:48), and a child below knowing has received none to answer for; David, losing his infant, said "I shall go to him" (2 Sam 12:23) and washed his face in hope. The infant-damning doctrines were men's systems overriding Christ's arms. Why do they die at all? Because the whole creation groans under the enemy's rule awaiting redemption -- and the Father's answer is not a syllogism but a Son who entered the ward, took the children up in His arms (Mark 10:16), and rose to empty every small grave at His voice.

question: "Why does God demand worship? Isn't that narcissism?"

sayings.quote: "...Thou shalt worship the Lord thy God, and him only shalt thou serve."
sayings.expo: Notice who is speaking and about whom: the Son, deflecting worship away from what is offered to him in the wilderness and up to the Father alone. The most exalted being in the story points the praise elsewhere. A narcissistic system does not train its prince to say "him only."

sayings.quote: "But the hour cometh, and now is, when the true worshippers shall worship the Father in spirit and in truth: for the Father seeketh such to worship him."
sayings.expo: What the Father seeks is defined: worship in spirit and in truth -- reality, not ritual; honesty, not flattery. Narcissists demand image-maintenance and punish honesty; this Father seeks truth-tellers and, in the same conversation, recruits one from a despised people with a broken past. He seeks worshipers the way a spring seeks the thirsty.

sayings.quote: "Were there not ten cleansed? but where are the nine?... Arise, go thy way: thy faith hath made thee whole."
sayings.expo: Ten lepers healed; one returns to give thanks -- and the missing nine lose nothing of their healing. No plague resumes, no punishment falls; the grief in the question is for what the nine missed: the one who returned got the encounter, the wholeness beyond the cure. Gratitude, in Christ's economy, completes the receiver, not the Giver.

reason: Worship is not God consuming praise; it is creatures aligning with the Source of their life -- as a plant "worships" the sun by turning toward what feeds it. The command is a prescription, not an appetite: a doctor who insists you take the one medicine is not vain, and joy itself is incomplete until expressed (no one calls a man narcissistic for wanting his children to love what will make them alive). And the Father's character test is public: narcissists sacrifice others to themselves; this God gave His Son for His enemies. The diagnosis fails on the evidence.

question: "Why did God create Satan -- and let the serpent into the garden?"

sayings.quote: "He was a murderer from the beginning, and abode not in the truth... When he speaketh a lie, he speaketh of his own: for he is a liar, and the father of it."
sayings.expo: "Abode not" is the hinge: to abandon the truth one must have stood in it. Christ's biography of the devil is a creature made in the light who left -- the lie is "of his own," self-authored, fathered by him and not by his Maker. God created a bright spirit with real freedom; the spirit manufactured the first lie. Origin of the being: God. Origin of the evil: him.

sayings.quote: "...An enemy hath done this... The enemy that sowed them is the devil."
sayings.expo: In Christ's own parable of why the field is mixed, the householder's seed is all good; the tares arrive by hostile sowing, at night, by "an enemy." Asked the objection's exact question -- where did the bad in the field come from? -- the Sower answers on the record: not from my hand. And the reapers' offer to purge immediately is refused for the wheat's sake (v29): the delay the objector resents is protection.

sayings.quote: "I beheld Satan as lightning fall from heaven."
sayings.expo: A fall witnessed -- from heaven, like lightning: sudden, luminous, downward. The devil is not God's dark half nor an eternal rival; he is a fallen subordinate whose defeat Christ announces as already visible, whose end is already scheduled in fire "prepared for the devil and his angels" (Matt 25:41) -- prepared for him, note: hell was never designed with men in mind.

reason: Why permit the tempter in the garden at all? Because untested love is untried metal: a choice with no live alternative is not a choice, and the Father wanted sons, not scenery. The tree was not a trap but the ballot box; the serpent's presence made the "no" real so the "yes" could be. Entrapment manufactures a crime the victim wouldn't otherwise commit -- but Eden stacked everything toward life: one prohibition, every other tree free, the command clear, the warning explicit. And when the choice fell wrong, the Judge walked in with a promise (Gen 3:15) before He pronounced a sentence -- entrapping officers do not do that.

question: "Can God make a rock so heavy He can't lift it? Doesn't omnipotence contradict itself?"

sayings.quote: "With men this is impossible; but with God all things are possible."
sayings.expo: Spoken about a real impossibility -- saving a wealth-bound soul -- not about logical party tricks. "All things are possible" in Scripture is always aimed at things: real states of affairs (salvation, resurrection, provision) beyond creaturely power. A "rock too heavy for omnipotence" is not a thing -- it is a grammatical knot, two claims canceling each other inside one phrase.

sayings.quote: "Abba, Father, all things are possible unto thee; take away this cup from me: nevertheless not what I will, but what thou wilt."
sayings.expo: Christ affirms unbounded power and, in the same sentence, bows to its governor: the Father's will and character. Omnipotence in Scripture is never raw arbitrariness; it is all-power wielded by a nature -- a God who "cannot lie" (Titus 1:2), cannot deny Himself, cannot be untrue. Those "cannots" are not weaknesses; they are what makes the power trustworthy rather than terrifying.

sayings.quote: "...It is written again, Thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God."
sayings.expo: The devil proposed a stunt -- leap, and force a rescue -- a manufactured test with no purpose but spectacle. Christ's answer names the category: contrived tests of God are refused on principle. The rock puzzle is the same species -- a scenario built solely to corner power in a word game. The refusal to perform inside rigged frames is itself the biblical posture.

reason: Omnipotence means all power to do all that power can do -- every genuine task, however vast. "A stone an almighty being cannot lift" describes no task at all: it is "a square circle" wearing physics clothes, self-contradiction dressed as a challenge. Refusing to instantiate nonsense is not a limit on power any more than refusing to draw a four-sided triangle is a limit on an artist. The interesting divine "cannots" are moral -- cannot lie, cannot break covenant -- and those are precisely why the power can be leaned on with your whole weight.
