question: "How could an infinite God become a finite man -- isn't the incarnation just incoherent?"

sayings.quote: "I came forth from the Father, and am come into the world: again, I leave the world, and go to the Father."
sayings.expo: Christ describes it not as infinite shrinking into finite, but as a journey: came forth, came in, leaves, returns. The Son who was "with God in the beginning" took up a real human life without ceasing to be the Son -- a veiling, not an annihilation, of glory. The infinite did not become finite; the infinite Person took a finite nature to Himself.

sayings.quote: "And Jesus increased in wisdom and stature, and in favour with God and man."
sayings.expo: The record states it plainly: He grew, learned, developed -- a genuine human childhood, real limits genuinely accepted. Not the contradiction the objection imagines but the astonishment the gospel proclaims: the Word through whom galaxies were framed consented to nurse, to learn carpentry, to ask questions. The self-limitation is voluntary and real ("he humbled himself," Phil 2:8) -- power choosing not to grasp, which is love's definition, not logic's violation.

sayings.quote: "...the glory which I had with thee before the world was."
sayings.expo: He asks to resume a glory He set aside -- proof the setting-aside was a self-veiling of what remained fully His, not a loss of His nature. Philippians names the mechanic: He "emptied himself" (kenosis) -- not of deity, but of its independent exercise; He "made himself of no reputation" and took "the form of a servant." The infinite Person lived a finite life while holding His nature in trust with the Father.

reason: The objection assumes the incarnation means the infinite nature turned into a finite one -- a genuine contradiction. But that is not the claim: the eternal Son, without ceasing to be who He is, took a full human nature and lived within its limits by choice. Analogies limp, but consider: an author can write himself into his own story as a character -- truly present on the page, genuinely limited by the plot -- without ceasing to be the author who holds the whole book. The incarnation is not "infinite = finite" (a contradiction) but "the infinite Person also lives finitely" (a wonder). And note the fit with all this gauntlet has shown: a Son truly divine yet saying "my Father is greater than I" (Round 5), with glory before the world yet growing in wisdom, worshiped yet worshiping -- the "problems" evaporate the moment you stop making Him the co-equal Most High and let Him be what He said He was: the Word made flesh, the sent Son, God with us. question: "Isn't the gospel just the promise of heaven and threat of hell -- fear to control people?"

sayings.expo: Christ states His mission's aim as abundant life now -- zōē perisson, life overflowing -- not merely deferred survival. The engine He names is not dread of the exit but richness of the road.

sayings.quote: "...the truth shall make you free."
sayings.expo: The stated product is freedom, won by knowing, not by intimidation. Control systems fear inquiry (Round 35); Christ commands it and promises liberty as its fruit. You cannot run a fear-cult and stake it on "know the truth" -- the two aims cancel, and He chose the second.

sayings.quote: "Fear not, little flock; for it is your Father's good pleasure to give you the kingdom."
sayings.expo: "Fear not" is the most repeated command He gives -- and here the reason is the Father's good pleasure to give, not His readiness to punish. question: "Isn't Christianity just a list of do's and don'ts -- joyless legalism?"

sayings.quote: "...Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart... and thy neighbour as thyself. On these two commandments hang all the law and the prophets."
sayings.expo: Christ compresses the entire moral universe into two loves -- not a rulebook but a relationship, with everything else hanging from it. The commands are not arbitrary hoops; they are what love looks like in specific situations. Reduce it to a checklist and you have already lost what He said it was.

sayings.quote: "Take my yoke upon you... For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light."
sayings.expo: His yoke is easy -- set directly against the scribes who "bind heavy burdens and grievous to be borne, and lay them on men's shoulders" (Matt 23:4). The joyless rule-pile the objection describes is precisely what Christ diagnosed and opposed; the Pharisees were the legalists, and He was their fiercest critic. He came to lift the load, not add to it.

sayings.quote: "The sabbath was made for man, and not man for the sabbath."
sayings.expo: The governing principle for every command: rules serve people, not the reverse. Where a regulation had been twisted into a cage (healing forbidden on the sabbath), Christ broke the cage and kept the gift. His quarrel was never with God's law but with its weaponization -- the "don't" that had forgotten the "for man" behind it.

The fences that look joyless are guardrails around real goods (the marriage bed, the sober mind, the honest tongue), and every one of them, kept from love, protects a joy the "freedom" it forbids would have destroyed. This is the Winebibber (Round 74) who feasted, the Lord who made 150 gallons for a wedding, whose first sign was a party running out of wine and whose promise is "that your joy might be full" (John 15:11). question: "Is sex before marriage actually wrong? Who does it hurt?"

sayings.quote: "...he which made them at the beginning made them male and female... and they twain shall be ONE FLESH."
sayings.expo: Christ ties the one-flesh union to the covenant frame -- leaving, cleaving, becoming one: sex is the seal of a total, permanent self-gift, not a recreational act. In His design the body's deepest "yes" belongs inside the vow it enacts; severed from the covenant, it speaks a promise the will has not made. The union was never meant to be casual because it was never merely physical.

sayings.quote: "...out of the heart proceed evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, FORNICATIONS... these are the things which defile a man."
sayings.expo: Christ names fornication (porneia -- sex outside marriage) explicitly among what defiles -- from His own mouth, not merely Paul's or Leviticus'. "Who does it hurt?" is answered at the source: it forms the heart, trains the self to take intimacy without covenant, and shapes what a person becomes. The harm is interior first, and interior harm is real harm.

sayings.quote: "...thou hast had five husbands; and he whom thou now hast is not thy husband... I that speak unto thee am he."
sayings.expo: To a woman whose sexual history was a wound, Christ named the truth without contempt -- and gave her living water and the first commission to a city. His way with sexual sin is neither the shame-mob nor the shrug: honesty about the harm, dignity for the person, an open door to new life. That is the model the "purity culture" and the "anything goes" crowd both miss.

The fences guard the good: they protect the union's meaning, the children it may make, and the trust it's built to carry. And the gospel meets the fallen -- nearly everyone stands somewhere on this road needing grace -- with the well-side pattern: no condemnation, real truth, living water, "go, and sin no more." Not a Bronze-Age hangup -- the Maker's manual for the most powerful bond He gave, and mercy for all who've used it otherwise.

question: "If God heals, why do believers still get sick and die? Isn't faith-healing a cruel scam?"

sayings.quote: "They that be whole need not a physician, but they that are sick."
sayings.expo: Christ speaks of the physician as a good, normal thing -- the sick rightly go to one; He builds a teaching on it without a trace of "real faith skips the doctor." Luke, who recorded much of His life, was "the beloved physician" (Col 4:14). Medicine is not the enemy of faith in Scripture; it is one of the Father's mercies, and using it is wisdom, not unbelief.

sayings.quote: "...thy faith hath made thee whole; go in peace."
sayings.expo: And He did heal, really -- publicly, bodily, sometimes through faith and sometimes to people who had none yet (the man at Bethesda didn't even know who He was, John 5:13). Healing is real and God still does it. But notice: Christ healed some and "could there do no mighty work" in unbelieving Nazareth (Mark 6:5) yet raised the dead among strangers -- healing tracked His Father's purpose, never a formula the sick could operate.

sayings.quote: "...My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness."
sayings.expo: The risen Christ's own answer to a healing prayer He declined: Paul asked thrice, the thorn stayed, the grace came instead. Scripture is not embarrassed by unhealed saints -- Paul "left Trophimus at Miletum sick" (2 Tim 4:20), told Timothy to take wine for his stomach (1 Tim 5:23). The blame-the-victim "not enough faith" doctrine is refuted by an apostle whose faith no one questions being told no.

reason: God heals -- by miracle when He wills, by medicine (His gift, worked through the physician He inspired to travel with Paul), and finally and certainly at the resurrection, where every disease loses. What Scripture never teaches is the faith-healer's lie: that healing is a lever the sick can pull with enough belief or enough "seed money" (Round 27's whip swings here too), so that failure to be healed is the sufferer's fault. That doctrine is cruelty and fraud, and it is condemned by Paul's thorn, Trophimus's sickbed, and Christ's own unremoved cup. Pray boldly for healing -- He invites it; use the doctor freely -- He gave him; and when the answer is "not yet" or "my grace instead," know it is the same Father who wept at a grave and then emptied it. The final healing is guaranteed; the timing is His.
argument:
Yeshua said, "They that be whole need not a physician, but they that are sick." (Matt 9:12). Christ speaks of the physician as a good, normal thing -- the sick rightly go to one; He builds a teaching on it without a trace of "real faith skips the doctor." Luke, who recorded much of His life, was "the beloved physician" (Col 4:14). Medicine is not the enemy of faith in Scripture; it is one of the Father's mercies, and using it is wisdom, not unbelief.

Yeshua said, "...thy faith hath made thee whole; go in peace." (Mark 5:34). And He did heal, really -- publicly, bodily, sometimes through faith and sometimes to people who had none yet (the man at Bethesda didn't even know who He was, John 5:13). Healing is real and God still does it. But notice: Christ healed some and "could there do no mighty work" in unbelieving Nazareth (Mark 6:5) yet raised the dead among strangers -- healing tracked His Father's purpose, never a formula the sick could operate.

question: "Is the prosperity gospel true -- does God want everyone rich and healthy?"

sayings.quote: "...The foxes have holes, and the birds of the air have nests; but the Son of man hath not where to lay his head."
sayings.expo: The Lord of glory chose poverty -- no house, no pillow guaranteed. If wealth were faith's reward, its perfect Exemplar would have been its richest man; instead He was homeless by choice. The prosperity gospel cannot survive one look at the material life of the Christ it claims to preach.

sayings.quote: "Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth... but lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven... For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also."
sayings.expo: Christ points the believer's ambition away from earthly accumulation, not toward it. The prosperity message aims the heart at exactly the treasure He said to stop storing -- it is not a variation of His teaching but its reversal, redirecting the affections He labored to lift heavenward.

sayings.quote: "...If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me."
sayings.expo: The promised path is a cross, not a Cadillac -- and "in the world ye shall have tribulation" (John 16:33) was said to His own. He never sold health-and-wealth; He offered Himself, and a road that costs. A gospel that removes the cross has removed the Christ and left only the marketing.

reason: The prosperity gospel inverts nearly everything: Christ was poor, His apostles hungry, imprisoned, and beaten (Paul's own résumé, 2 Cor 11:23-27), and the verdict is "godliness with contentment is great gain... having food and raiment let us be therewith content" (1 Tim 6:6-8). The "seed-faith" lever -- give to get, believe to bank -- is the money-changers' table rebuilt in a studio (Round 27's whip swings here), and its cruelty is the blame it lays on the sick and the poor, calling their suffering a faith-failure -- the exact "not enough faith" lie Paul's thorn refutes (Round 95). God does provide (Matt 6:33), and to some He entrusts wealth as stewardship (Round 77); but He guarantees no one riches or health as belief's payout, for that makes Him a vending machine and Job, Paul, and Christ Himself its biggest failures. The treasure He promises is Himself -- and that one never fails to arrive.

question: "Is gambling or playing the lottery a sin? The Bible never mentions it."

sayings.quote: "No man can serve two masters... Ye cannot serve God and mammon."
sayings.expo: Gambling is devotion to mammon fused with trust in chance -- the exact rival mastership Christ names as mutually exclusive with God. Its thrill is the hope of money-from-nothing; its faith is in luck. The habit trains the heart to look to the wheel where the disciple is to look to the Father.

sayings.quote: "...Take heed, and beware of covetousness: for a man's life consisteth not in the abundance of the things which he possesseth."
sayings.expo: The engine of gambling is precisely covetousness -- wanting more, for nothing, faster. Christ warns against it in the same breath He warns against measuring life by possessions. The lottery sells the rich-fool's fantasy (Round 77) as a dollar ticket: my barns, bigger, by luck -- and "this night thy soul."

sayings.quote: "...for even the Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life..."
sayings.expo: Christ's economy runs on giving, not extracting -- and gambling's structure is the opposite: my gain is another's loss, prosperity harvested from a neighbor's ruin. Set against "labour, working with his hands... that he may have to give to him that needeth" (Eph 4:28), the wager reverses the whole direction: take from many, by chance, to enrich one.

reason: No verse says "thou shalt not gamble" -- but the principles converge like a vise: it feeds covetousness (Luke 12:15), trusts luck over the Father (Matt 6:24), seeks gain from a neighbor's loss (against love-thy-neighbor and honest labor, Eph 4:28), and -- the quiet cruelty -- preys on the poor, for the lottery is a tax on the desperate, heaviest where hope is thinnest. A dollar ticket is not the unforgivable sin, and this is a matter for a governed conscience, not a new commandment; but the disposition it cultivates -- something-for-nothing, luck over labor, my windfall from your loss -- is the precise inverse of the trust, work, and generosity Christ commends. The wise steward invests and gives (the talents, Matt 25); the gambler covets and takes. Ask not "is there a rule?" but "which heart is this feeding?"

question: "Does cremation affect the resurrection? Is burial required?"

sayings.quote: "...all that are in the graves shall hear his voice, and shall come forth..."
sayings.expo: The resurrection is an act of God's re-creating word -- "shall hear his voice" -- not a mortician's reassembly of preserved parts. The same voice that called light out of nothing and Lazarus out of decay calls the dead forth; it is not searching for atoms. What raises you is His power, not your preservation.

sayings.quote: "...fear him which is able to destroy both soul and body..."
sayings.expo: God's power over the body is total -- able to destroy it utterly, and therefore infinitely able to remake it. A God who can un-create can re-create; ashes are no harder to Him than dust. The objection imagines a God limited by chemistry; Christ describes one who authored chemistry and is not bound by it.

sayings.quote: "...I am the God of Abraham... God is not the God of the dead, but of the living."
sayings.expo: The resurrection rests on God's faithfulness and power, not the corpse's condition -- Abraham, dust for millennia, is secured because God remains his God. Identity is kept by the Father who holds it (Round 65), not by an intact body in a box. The patriarchs are long since dust, and their rising is certain.

reason: Every buried body becomes dust too -- "dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return" (Gen 3:19); cremation only hastens what the grave completes, so if ashes could block the resurrection, no one buried more than a generation would rise either. And Paul settles the mechanism: the body sown is not the body raised -- "thou sowest not that body that shall be... God giveth it a body as it hath pleased him" (1 Cor 15:37-38); a seed dies and God grows something new and glorious, not a reassembled corpse. The martyrs burned at the stake, the saints lost at sea, the faithful dust of forty centuries -- all rise at the Voice. Burial beautifully pictures that hope (a seed sown, awaiting spring), which is why the church has loved it; but it is conscience and reverence, not a salvation requirement. What matters is that the person is kept by the Father and raised at the Son's word -- and no fire, sea, or grave has ever been able to hide one of His from Him.

question: "All right -- then what must I actually DO to be saved?"

sayings.quote: "...The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand: REPENT ye, and BELIEVE the gospel."
sayings.expo: His opening sermon is the whole answer in two verbs: repent -- turn from your sins, naming them, meaning it -- and believe the good news of the Son. Not a maze; a turning and a trusting. Everything else in the Christian life grows from this root, but this is the door, stated by Christ in His first recorded words.

sayings.quote: "...this is life eternal, that they might know thee the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom thou hast sent."
sayings.expo: Salvation is defined as knowing -- the Father as the only true God, and Yeshua whom He sent. It is relationship, not a transaction cleared; a Person known, honored, trusted. Honor the Father as the one true God, receive the Son He sent -- that is the substance the two verbs open into.

sayings.quote: "...how much more shall your heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to them that ASK him?"
sayings.expo: And the certain gift, for the certain asking: ask the Father for the Holy Spirit -- persistently, aloud, in your own closet (Matt 6:6) -- and it is the one request He promises to answer every time. The new birth (Round 54) comes as the Father breathes His own life into the one who turns, trusts, and asks. You do not manufacture it; you ask, and He gives.

reason: Here is the plain path, and it is plainer than the confusion suggests: Repent -- name your sins to the Father and turn from them. Believe on the Son whom He sent, trusting His ransom, not your record. Honor the Father as the only true God (John 17:3). Ask Him, out loud and in earnest, for the Holy Spirit (Luke 11:13) -- and keep asking until He fills you. Then walk it out in living faith that bears fruit (Round 55), begun now and kept by enduring (Round 56). That is it -- no maze, no gatekeeper, no fee (Round 27). The churches differ on the trimmings; the door has always been the same two verbs Christ preached first. You can do it today, in this room, in your own words -- "whosoever shall call upon the name of the Lord shall be saved," and He is not far from any one of us.

question: "Why does any of this even matter? What difference would Jesus make to my actual life?"

sayings.quote: "I am come that they might have life, and that they might have it more abundantly."
sayings.expo: The difference He offers is not an extra layer of obligation but a different quality of being alive -- life abundant, life that death cannot end. Not more rules on top of your existence, but your existence set on a new foundation: known by a Father, freed from the ledger, aimed at something that outlasts you.

sayings.quote: "Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you REST... and ye shall find rest unto your souls."
sayings.expo: To the one who gets up, works, and carries it all: rest -- not from the work, but in the soul beneath it. The striving to be enough, to justify yourself, to outrun the fear of the end -- He offers to carry it. "Guilt I don't need" assumes the guilt is His invention; He offers instead to take it away, which is the opposite of adding it.

sayings.quote: "Behold, I stand at the door, and knock: if any man hear my voice, and open the door, I will come in to him..."
sayings.expo: The risen Christ's posture toward you right now: knocking, not barging -- the whole thing waits on a door only you can open, from the inside. It is not an obligation imposed but a Person requesting entrance, into the ordinary life you already have -- the getting up, the working, the loving of your people -- to fill it with the One who made you for Himself.

reason: The difference is everything these hundred rounds have traced: a real Father instead of an indifferent void; forgiveness instead of the ledger you can never balance; the Spirit's own presence in you now, not merely a code to obey; your work, your love, your people lifted from "then I die" into a story that death cannot close; and death itself disarmed into sleep-before-morning (Round 65). You can live decently without Him -- many do, on borrowed light (the very kindness, dignity, and love-of-neighbor you value are His fingerprints, Round 83). But the question was never whether you can be respectable; it is whether you are known, forgiven, and kept -- and whether the love that pursued you all the way to a cross gets an answer. The ninety-nine objections were the fence around a door; the door is a Person, and He is knocking. He that hath ears to hear, let him hear.
